messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 64
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: Latin American
- Relationship Status: Divorced
- Occupation: Jeweler
- Trauma Type: Witnessed domestic violence (childhood)
- Pcl5: 36

# The Weight of Silence

Miguel is a 64-year-old Colombian-born jeweler who has spent the better part of four decades crafting delicate things — rings, pendants, the kind of objects people give each other on the days they most want to be remembered. He works alone in a small shop in the back of a strip mall, and he prefers it that way. The solitude, he says, is something he earned.

He grew up in Medellín in the 1960s and 70s, the eldest of five children in a household ruled by his father's moods. His father was not always violent — that is something Miguel is careful to say — but when he drank, the apartment became a different place entirely. Miguel remembers being perhaps seven or eight the first time he watched his father strike his mother across the face hard enough to knock her into the kitchen doorframe. He remembers the sound more than anything. He stood frozen in the hallway in his undershirt, certain that if he moved, something worse would happen. He learned to read the evenings the way other children learn to read books — the particular weight of footsteps on the stairs, the smell of aguardiente, the pitch of his mother's voice when she was trying to make herself small. He became very good at staying still.

The violence continued through his adolescence, episodic and unpredictable, and Miguel left home at seventeen. He eventually immigrated to the United States in his late twenties, married, built a life. For long stretches of time, he believed he had simply moved on. His marriage lasted eleven years before his wife told him she felt like she was living with someone who was never fully present. He did not argue with her. He knew she was right.

What he did not understand, until recently, was how much of his daily life was still organized around that hallway in Medellín. He startles badly at sudden sounds — a door slamming in the shop next door, a car backfiring in the parking lot — and the rush of alarm that moves through him feels entirely disproportionate, embarrassing for a man his age. He has trouble sleeping most nights, lying awake with a low, sourceless dread that he cannot think his way out of. When he does sleep, he sometimes wakes from dreams he cannot fully remember, only that his mother was in them, and that he was too small to help.

He finds the work of jewelry-making both a refuge and, occasionally, a trap. The concentration it demands quiets his mind in a way little else does, and he takes genuine pride in the precision his hands still carry. But there are moments — when a customer raises their voice over a repair estimate, or when he hears a couple arguing in the parking lot — when something shifts in him abruptly. His chest tightens. He sets down his tools. He has learned to excuse himself to the back room until it passes.

He describes himself as a man who has always handled things on his own, and he says this without self-pity, as a simple statement of fact. He has few close friendships. His adult children live in other states and he speaks to them with a warmth that is genuine but careful, as if intimacy is a distance he is always measuring. He worries sometimes that he passed something on to them — some vigilance, some habit of bracing — and this thought troubles him more than most.

He came to therapy not because of a crisis but because of an accumulation. He turned 64 in the spring and found himself thinking about his father, who died at 71, and about how many years he has spent standing very still in a hallway, waiting for something terrible to happen. He is tired of waiting. He would like, he says quietly, to put down whatever it is he has been carrying. He is not entirely sure yet what that would feel like.
